docs.title: 9.4 复杂性类别
docs.text: 级别：第 9 级 · 算法理论与计算边界 状态：已展开。

docs.title: 学习目标
docs.text:
• 定义 P、NP、coNP；
  • 区分“求解”与“验证”；
  • 理解 NP 难/NP 完全。

docs.title: P 与 NP
docs.text:
• P：存在多项式时间算法求解的判定问题；
  • NP：存在多项式时间验证器，给定证书可在多项式时间内验证“是”；
  • coNP：补问题在 NP 中。
\[ P\subseteq NP,\qquad P\subseteq coNP. \]

是否 \(P=NP\) 未解决。

docs.title: 验证器
docs.text:
以 SAT 为例，证书是一个赋值：

1def verify_sat(clauses: list[list[int]], assignment: dict[int,bool]) -> bool:
2    for clause in clauses:
3        if not any(assignment.get(abs(lit), False) == (lit > 0) for lit in clause):
4            return False
5    return True

验证 \(O(\text{子句总长度})\)；但找赋值可能指数。

docs.title: NP 难与 NP 完全
docs.text:
• \(L\) 是 NP 难：所有 NP 问题 \(\le_p L\)；
  • \(L\) 是 NP 完全：\(L\in NP\) 且 NP 难；
  • SAT 是第一个被证明 NP 完全的问题（Cook–Levin）。

docs.title: C++ 验证器
docs.text:
1#include <vector>
 2
 3bool verify_sat(const std::vector<std::vector<int>>& clauses,
 4                const std::vector<int>& value) {
 5    for (const auto& clause : clauses) {
 6        bool ok = false;
 7        for (int lit : clause) {
 8            bool v = value[std::abs(lit)] != 0;
 9            if ((lit > 0) == v) { ok = true; break; }
10        }
11        if (!ok) return false;
12    }
13    return true;
14}

docs.title: 边界
docs.text: 概念 注意 NP 只要求“是”有短证书 coNP 不是 NP 的补集定义 NP 难 不要求属于 NP 指数时间 NP 不排除指数算法

docs.text:

  2. 说明为什么“验证快”不等于“求解快”。
  3. 举例一个 coNP 问题。

docs.title: 9.5 NP 完全问题
docs.text: 级别：第 9 级 · 算法理论与计算边界 状态：已展开。

docs.title: 学习目标
docs.text:
• 认识 SAT、3-SAT、团、顶点覆盖、子集和；
  • 用小规模求解器验证；
  • 理解归约链。

docs.title: 经典 NP 完全问题
docs.text:
• SAT：布尔公式可满足性；
  • 3-SAT：每个子句恰 3 个字面量；
  • 团：图是否有大小 \(k\) 的完全子图；
  • 顶点覆盖：是否有大小 \(k\) 的点覆盖所有边；
  • 子集和：是否有子集和等于目标。

docs.title: 小规模 SAT 求解
docs.text:
1from itertools import product
2
3def sat_bruteforce(n: int, clauses: list[list[int]]) -> list[bool] | None:
4    for bits in product([False, True], repeat=n):
5        if all(any(bits[abs(l)-1] == (l > 0) for l in c) for c in clauses):
6            return list(bits)
7    return None

\(O(2^n\cdot m)\)；只适合很小的 \(n\)。

docs.title: 归约链
docs.text:
\[ \text{SAT}\le_p\text{3-SAT}\le_p\text{独立集}\le_p\text{顶点覆盖}. \]

每一步都要保持答案，并在多项式时间内构造。

docs.title: 顶点覆盖暴力
docs.text:
1from itertools import combinations
2
3def has_vertex_cover(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int,int]], k: int) -> bool:
4    for chosen in combinations(range(n), k):
5        s = set(chosen)
6        if all(u in s or v in s for u, v in edges):
7            return True
8    return False

docs.title: C++ 子集和
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2#include <vector>
 3
 4bool subset_sum(const std::vector<int>& a, int target) {
 5    std::vector<bool> dp(target + 1, false);
 6    dp[0] = true;
 7    for (int x : a)
 8        for (int j = target; j >= x; --j)
 9            dp[j] = dp[j] || dp[j-x];
10    return dp[target];
11}

注意：这是伪多项式 \(O(n\cdot target)\)，不是多项式。

docs.title: 边界
docs.text: 场景 注意 小 \(n\) 暴力/回溯可行 大 \(n\) 需要近似/参数化/启发式 伪多项式 target 的位数是指数 归约 参数与图构造

  3. 说明子集和 DP 为什么不是多项式时间。

docs.title: 9.6 算法下界
docs.text: 级别：第 9 级 · 算法理论与计算边界 状态：已展开。

docs.title: 学习目标
docs.text:
• 用决策树证明比较排序下界；
  • 理解对抗论证；
  • 区分“下界”与“最优算法”。

docs.title: 比较排序下界
docs.text:
比较排序的决策树有 \(n!\) 个叶子；二叉树高度至少 \(\log_2(n!)=\Omega(n\log n)\)。

所以任何基于比较的排序最坏情况至少 \(\Omega(n\log n)\) 次比较。

docs.title: 计数比较
docs.text:
1def insertion_sort_count(a: list[int]) -> tuple[list[int], int]:
 2    a = a[:]
 3    cmp = 0
 4    for i in range(1, len(a)):
 5        x = a[i]
 6        j = i - 1
 7        while j >= 0:
 8            cmp += 1
 9            if a[j] <= x:
10                break
11            a[j+1] = a[j]
12            j -= 1
13        a[j+1] = x
14    return a, cmp

对逆序数组，比较次数 \(\Theta(n^2)\)；下界只说明“至少”，不说明某个算法达到。

docs.title: 对抗论证
docs.text: 对手每次回答都让算法保留尽可能多的可能性；若每次只能排除常数比例，至少需要 \(\Omega(\log N)\) 次。

docs.title: 其他下界
docs.text:
• 查找无序数组：\(\Omega(n)\)；
  • 比较模型找最大：\(n-1\) 次比较；
  • 某些数据结构操作有摊还下界。

docs.title: C++ 比较计数
docs.text:
1#include <algorithm>
 2#include <iostream>
 3#include <vector>
 4
 5int main() {
 6    std::vector<int> a{5,4,3,2,1};
 7    int cmp = 0;
 8    std::sort(a.begin(), a.end(), [&](int x, int y) { ++cmp; return x < y; });
 9    std::cout << cmp << '\n';
10}

docs.title: 边界
docs.text: 场景 注意 非比较排序 下界不适用 最坏/平均 下界通常指最坏 模型 RAM/比较/图灵机不同 下界证明 不等于算法实现

  3. 设计一个对抗策略证明某问题下界。

docs.title: 9.7 近似算法
docs.text: 级别：第 9 级 · 算法理论与计算边界 状态：已展开。

docs.title: 学习目标
docs.text:
• 定义近似比；
  • 写顶点覆盖 2-近似；
  • 用贪心做集合覆盖。

docs.title: 近似比
docs.text:
对最小化问题，算法解 \(A\) 与最优解 \(OPT\) 满足

\[ A\le \rho\cdot OPT \]

称 \(\rho\)-近似。\(\rho\) 越接近 1 越好。

docs.title: 顶点覆盖 2-近似
docs.text:
反复取一条未覆盖边，把两个端点都加入覆盖。

 1def vertex_cover_2approx(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int,int]]) -> set[int]:
 2    cover = set()
 3    used = [False] * len(edges)
 4    for i, (u, v) in enumerate(edges):
 5        if used[i]:
 6            continue
 7        cover.add(u); cover.add(v)
 8        for j, (a, b) in enumerate(edges):
 9            if a in cover or b in cover:
10                used[j] = True
11    return cover

近似比 2：每次选的边至少有一个端点必须在任何覆盖中，而我们选了两个。

docs.title: 集合覆盖贪心
docs.text: 每步选覆盖未覆盖元素最多的集合；近似比 \(H_n=O(\log n)\)。

docs.title: C++ 顶点覆盖
docs.text:
1#include <set>
 2#include <utility>
 3#include <vector>
 4
 5std::set<int> vertex_cover(const std::vector<std::pair<int,int>>& edges) {
 6    std::set<int> cover;
 7    for (auto [u, v] : edges) {
 8        if (cover.count(u) || cover.count(v)) continue;
 9        cover.insert(u); cover.insert(v);
10    }
11    return cover;
12}

docs.title: 边界
docs.text: 场景 注意 最大化问题 比值方向相反 近似比 最坏情况保证 启发式 无保证，不是近似算法 不可近似性 某些问题有下界

docs.title: 9.8 在线算法
docs.text: 级别：第 9 级 · 算法理论与计算边界 状态：已展开。

docs.title: 学习目标
docs.text:
• 理解在线决策与竞争比；
  • 分析 ski rental；
  • 了解缓存替换。

docs.title: 竞争比
docs.text:
在线算法 \(ALG\) 与离线最优 \(OPT\) 满足

\[ ALG\le c\cdot OPT \]

称 \(c\)-竞争。输入顺序未知，不能回退。

docs.title: Ski rental
docs.text:
滑雪者每次租雪板花 1，买雪板花 \(B\)。不知道会滑几次。

策略：先租 \(B-1\) 次，之后买。

  • 若总次数 \(<B\)：花费 \(k\le B-1\)，最优也是 \(k\)；
  • 若总次数 \(\ge B\)：花费 \((B-1)+B=2B-1\)，最优 \(B\)；
  • 竞争比 \(<2\)。
1def ski_rental(days: int, buy: int) -> int:
2    cost = 0
3    for _ in range(days):
4        if cost < buy - 1:
5            cost += 1
6        else:
7            return cost + buy
8    return cost

docs.title: 缓存替换
docs.text:
• FIFO/LRU：确定性；
  • 随机标记算法：\(O(\log k)\) 竞争；
  • 离线最优需要知道未来。

docs.title: C++ LRU 简化
docs.text:
1#include <list>
 2#include <unordered_map>
 3
 4class LRU {
 5    int cap;
 6    std::list<int> order;
 7    std::unordered_map<int, std::list<int>::iterator> pos;
 8public:
 9    explicit LRU(int c) : cap(c) {}
10    void access(int x) {
11        if (pos.count(x)) order.erase(pos[x]);
12        else if (static_cast<int>(order.size()) == cap) { pos.erase(order.back()); order.pop_back(); }
13        order.push_front(x);
14        pos[x] = order.begin();
15    }
16};

docs.title: 边界
docs.text: 场景 注意 输入顺序 在线算法不能重排 竞争比 最坏情况 随机化 期望竞争比 缓存大小 \(k=0\) 特判

docs.title: 9.9 参数化算法
docs.text: 级别：第 9 级 · 算法理论与计算边界 状态：已展开。

docs.title: 学习目标
docs.text:
• 定义 FPT；
  • 用搜索树解顶点覆盖；
  • 了解核化。

docs.title: 参数化复杂度
docs.text:
问题实例带参数 \(k\)；若算法时间

\[ O(f(k)\cdot n^c) \]

其中 \(c\) 与 \(k\) 无关，称固定参数可解（FPT）。

docs.title: 顶点覆盖搜索树
docs.text:
选一条边 \((u,v)\)，任何覆盖必含 \(u\) 或 \(v\)：

 1def vertex_cover_fpt(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int,int]], k: int) -> set[int] | None:
 2    if not edges:
 3        return set()
 4    if k == 0:
 5        return None
 6    u, v = edges[0]
 7    rest = [e for e in edges if u not in e and v not in e]
 8    left = vertex_cover_fpt(n, rest, k - 1)
 9    if left is not None:
10        return left | {u}
11    right = vertex_cover_fpt(n, rest, k - 1)
12    if right is not None:
13        return right | {v}
14    return None

时间 \(O(2^k\cdot m)\)。

docs.title: 核化
docs.text: 用规则把实例缩小到大小只依赖 \(k\) 的核；例如顶点覆盖中度数 \(>k\) 的点必选。

docs.title: C++ 递归框架
docs.text:
1#include <utility>
 2#include <vector>
 3
 4bool vc(int k, std::vector<std::pair<int,int>> edges) {
 5    if (edges.empty()) return true;
 6    if (k == 0) return false;
 7    auto [u, v] = edges.front();
 8    std::vector<std::pair<int,int>> rest;
 9    for (auto e : edges) if (e.first != u && e.second != u && e.first != v && e.second != v) rest.push_back(e);
10    return vc(k-1, rest);
11}

（示例只探索一侧；完整版需分别尝试 \(u\)、\(v\)。）

docs.title: 边界
docs.text: 场景 注意 \(k\) 大 \(2^k\) 爆炸 参数选择 影响 FPT 核大小 需证明规则安全 NP 难 参数化不改变最坏情况

docs.title: 9.10 随机计算理论
docs.text: 级别：第 9 级 · 算法理论与计算边界 状态：已展开。

docs.title: 学习目标
docs.text:
• 区分 Monte Carlo / Las Vegas；
  • 定义 RP、BPP、ZPP；
  • 用重复多数降低错误率。

docs.title: 类别
docs.text:
• RP：多项式时间，正确答案为“是”时至少 \(1/2\) 接受；“否”一定拒绝；
  • coRP：对“否”有单侧保证；
  • ZPP：Las Vegas，期望多项式时间，结果总正确；
  • BPP：双侧错误，错误率 \(\le1/3\)。
\[ RP\subseteq BPP,\qquad ZPP=RP\cap coRP. \]

docs.title: 错误放大
docs.text:
若单次错误率 \(p<1/2\)，独立重复 \(2t+1\) 次取多数，错误率指数下降（Chernoff）。

1import random
2
3def majority_vote(f, trials: int = 101) -> bool:
4    return sum(f() for _ in range(trials)) * 2 > trials

docs.title: 例：随机化素性测试
docs.text: Miller–Rabin 是 Monte Carlo：合数可能被误判为素数，重复 \(k\) 次把错误率降到 \(4^{-k}\)。

docs.title: C++ 重复实验
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2#include <random>
 3
 4int main() {
 5    std::mt19937 rng(12345);
 6    std::bernoulli_distribution coin(0.5);
 7    int yes = 0, trials = 10000;
 8    for (int i = 0; i < trials; ++i) yes += coin(rng);
 9    std::cout << static_cast<double>(yes) / trials << '\n';
10}

docs.title: 边界
docs.text: 场景 注意 单侧/双侧 错误方向不同 独立性 重复需独立 随机源 伪随机 vs 真随机 去随机化 某些问题可确定性化

docs.title: 练习
docs.text:
1. 证明重复多数把错误率指数降低。

docs.title: Writing conventions
docs.text:
• Give the problem and the interface first, then the implementation;
  • The Python version expresses the algorithm structure first;
  • The C++ version demonstrates pointers, memory layout, ownership and resource management;
  • Each chapter contains at least: normal cases, boundary cases, complexity analysis, exercises.

docs.title: 1.1 Algorithm and Program
docs.text: Level: Level 1 · Programming and Algorithms: Getting Started Status: expanded (concept, dual-language implementations, boundary cases, exercises).

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• explain clearly what distinguishes an "algorithm" from a "program";
  • decompose a problem into input, processing, and output;
  • describe the steps in pseudocode, then implement them in Python and in C++ respectively;
  • test a program with an empty input, a single element, and duplicate values.

docs.title: Algorithms and Programs
docs.text:
An algorithm is a finite sequence of steps that solves a class of problems: every step must have a precise meaning, execution must stop after finitely many steps, and a valid output must be produced. A program is a concrete implementation of an algorithm in some language; the same algorithm may have different programs.

Describing an algorithm requires stating at least:

  1. Input: which data are allowed, and how large the input may be;
  2. Output: what constitutes a legal result;
  3. Process: what each step does;
  4. Termination: why it is guaranteed to stop;
  5. Correctness: why the output satisfies the requirements.

docs.title: Example: sum, maximum, count
docs.text:
Given an integer array \(a\), compute respectively:

  • the sum of all elements;
  • the maximum element;
  • the number of elements satisfying \(a_i>0\).

Pseudocode:

1sum ← 0
2maximum ← a[0]
3positive ← 0
4for each x in a:
5    sum ← sum + x
6    if x > maximum: maximum ← x
7    if x > 0: positive ← positive + 1
8return (sum, maximum, positive)

This pseudocode assumes a non-empty array; the maximum of an empty array is undefined and must be handled separately. This is the first appearance of "boundary conditions".

docs.title: Python Implementation
docs.text:
1def summarize(a: list[int]) -> tuple[int, int, int] | None:
 2    """Return (sum, maximum, positive_count); None for an empty list."""
 3    if not a:
 4        return None
 5    total = 0
 6    maximum = a[0]
 7    positive = 0
 8    for x in a:
 9        total += x
10        if x > maximum:
11            maximum = x
12        if x > 0:
13            positive += 1
14    return total, maximum, positive
15
16
17if __name__ == "__main__":
18    print(summarize([3, -1, 4, 0, 5]))  # (11, 5, 3)
19    print(summarize([]))                # None

docs.title: C++ Implementation
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2#include <optional>
 3#include <vector>
 4
 5struct Summary {
 6    long long sum;
 7    int maximum;
 8    int positive;
 9};
10
11std::optional<Summary> summarize(const std::vector<int>& a) {
12    if (a.empty()) return std::nullopt;
13    long long sum = 0;
14    int maximum = a[0];
15    int positive = 0;
16    for (int x : a) {
17        sum += x;
18        if (x > maximum) maximum = x;
19        if (x > 0) ++positive;
20    }
21    return Summary{sum, maximum, positive};
22}
23
24int main() {
25    auto r = summarize({3, -1, 4, 0, 5});
26    if (r) std::cout << r->sum << ' ' << r->maximum << ' ' << r->positive << '\n';
27    auto empty = summarize({});
28    std::cout << (empty ? "value" : "empty") << '\n';
29}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• Time: \(O(n)\), since each element is scanned only once;
  • Extra space: \(O(1)\) (excluding the input and the returned structure).

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Input Expected [] explicitly return "no result"; a[0] must not be accessed [0] sum=0, max=0, positive=0 [-5] sum=-5, max=-5, positive=0 [1, 1, 1] duplicate values do not affect the result

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Add "minimum" and "count of even numbers", still keeping \(O(n)\) time and \(O(1)\) space.
  2. If the array length can reach \(10^6\), how does Python's sum differ from a hand-written loop? Measure it.
  3. Write a version that raises an exception on empty input instead of returning None; explain the trade-off in interface design.

docs.title: 1.2 Variables and Types
docs.text: Level: Level 1 · Programming and Algorithms: Getting Started Status: expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• distinguish integers, floating-point numbers, booleans, characters, and strings;
  • understand the difference between Python's dynamic typing and C++'s static typing;
  • know where integer overflow, floating-point error, and implicit conversion cause problems.

docs.title: Python: Objects and Names
docs.text:
A Python variable is a name bound to an object; the type belongs to the object, not to the name.

1x = 42          # int
2x = "forty-two" # now bound to str
3print(type(x))  # <class 'str'>

Python integers can in principle be arbitrarily large; floating-point numbers are IEEE 754 double precision and cannot represent 0.1 exactly.

1print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)  # False
2print(abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-12)  # True

docs.title: C++: Types and Objects
docs.text:
A C++ variable has a static type, fixed at compile time; an assignment must be convertible to that type.

 1#include <iostream>
 2#include <string>
 3
 4int main() {
 5    int x = 42;
 6    // x = "forty-two"; // compile error
 7    double d = 0.1 + 0.2;
 8    std::cout << (d == 0.3) << '\n'; // usually prints 0
 9    std::string s = std::to_string(x);
10    std::cout << s << '\n';
11}

docs.title: Integer Range and Overflow
docs.text:
int is usually 32 bits, with a range of roughly \(-2.1\times10^9\) to \(2.1\times10^9\). Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C++, so "wraparound" must not be relied upon.

1#include <limits>
2#include <iostream>
3
4int main() {
5    std::cout << std::numeric_limits<int>::max() << '\n';
6    long long safe = 1LL * 2000000000 + 2000000000;
7    std::cout << safe << '\n';
8}

Accumulation, products, and index computations can all overflow; both in contests and in engineering you should estimate the upper bound and use long long or Python integers when necessary.

docs.title: Type Conversion
docs.text:
• Python: int("12"), float("1.5"), str(3); on failure a ValueError is raised.
  • C++: std::stoi, std::stod, std::to_string; on failure an exception is thrown (std::invalid_argument / std::out_of_range).

Do not use C-style casts to "fix" type errors; check the input range first, then convert explicitly.

docs.title: Booleans and Characters
docs.text:
• Python's bool is a subclass of int, and True == 1; do not rely on this for arithmetic.
  • C++'s bool converts to 0/1, but conversions between char and int are easily confused.
  • A string is not an array of characters: Python's str is immutable; C++'s std::string is mutable.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note int accumulation approaching \(2^{31}-1\) use long long or check in advance floating-point comparison use a tolerance, not == directly converting an empty string to a number stoi("") throws; int("") raises ValueError converting a negative number to unsigned may yield a huge value in C++; avoid mixing the two

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Read an integer and output the number of 1s in its binary representation; do it in both Python and C++.
  2. Compute \(1+2+\cdots+n\), and for \(n=10^9\) compare the result types and the running time in Python and C++.
  3. Write a safe parse_int that reports distinct error messages for an empty string, non-digits, and overflow.

docs.title: 1.3 Conditions and Loops
docs.text: Level: Level 1 · Programming and Algorithms: Getting Started Status: expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• use conditions to express classification;
  • use loops to express repetition, and state the termination condition;
  • identify the number of operations performed by nested loops.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
1def classify(x: int) -> str:
2    if x < 0:
3        return "negative"
4    if x == 0:
5        return "zero"
6    return "positive"

C++'s if has the same structure, but beware of = versus ==, and of the distinction between integers and booleans.

1#include <string>
2
3std::string classify(int x) {
4    if (x < 0) return "negative";
5    if (x == 0) return "zero";
6    return "positive";
7}

The three branches must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive. If they are written as two independent if statements, check whether any case is missing or duplicated.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
1def sum_to(n: int) -> int:
 2    total = 0
 3    i = 1
 4    while i <= n:
 5        total += i
 6        i += 1
 7    return total
 8
 9def sum_to_for(n: int) -> int:
10    total = 0
11    for i in range(1, n + 1):
12        total += i
13    return total

C++:

1long long sum_to(int n) {
2    long long total = 0;
3    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) total += i;
4    return total;
5}

docs.title: Termination
docs.text: A while loop must move its condition closer to false on every iteration; otherwise it loops forever. The i += 1 above is precisely that progress measure.

docs.title: Nested Loops
docs.text:
1def count_pairs(n: int) -> int:
2    count = 0
3    for i in range(n):
4        for j in range(i + 1, n):
5            count += 1
6    return count

The inner loop executes \((n-1)+(n-2)+\cdots+0=n(n-1)/2\) times, so the time complexity is \(O(n^2)\).

docs.title: Example: Primality Test
docs.text:
1def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
2    if n < 2:
3        return False
4    d = 2
5    while d * d <= n:
6        if n % d == 0:
7            return False
8        d += 1
9    return True

Only divisors up to \(\sqrt n\) are checked; when d * d might overflow, use d <= n // d instead.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Input Note n=0 the loop body never executes; range(1,1) is empty negative numbers range(1, n+1) is empty, which is not an error the prime 2 the loop condition 2*2<=2 is false, so True is returned large-integer multiplication d*d may overflow in C++

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Output all numbers from 1 to 100 that are divisible by 3 or by 5, but not by both.
  2. Compute \(n!\) with a loop, and handle \(n=0\).
  3. Count the pairs with \(1\le i<j\le n\) and \(\gcd(i,j)=1\); first write an \(O(n^2\log n)\) version, then think about how to optimise it.

docs.title: 1.4 Functions
docs.text: Level: Level 1 · Programming and Algorithms: Getting Started Status: expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• use a function to encapsulate a reusable step;
  • distinguish parameters, return values, and local variables;
  • understand the difference between pass-by-value, pass-by-reference, and object references.

docs.title: Function Contracts
docs.text:
A function must state at least:

  • the types and meaning of its parameters;
  • the return type and its valid range;
  • the preconditions (for example, that the array is non-empty);
  • whether it modifies its parameters.
1def average(values: list[float]) -> float:
2    if not values:
3        raise ValueError("average() requires a non-empty list")
4    return sum(values) / len(values)

In C++ the return type and the parameter types must be written explicitly:

1#include <stdexcept>
2#include <vector>
3
4double average(const std::vector<double>& values) {
5    if (values.empty()) throw std::invalid_argument("empty vector");
6    double sum = 0.0;
7    for (double x : values) sum += x;
8    return sum / static_cast<double>(values.size());
9}

const& denotes a read-only reference: the whole vector is not copied, and modification inside the function is not permitted.

docs.title: Local Variables and Scope
docs.text:
1def f(x: int) -> int:
2    y = x * 2      # local variable
3    return y
4
5# print(y)  # NameError

Variables inside a function disappear once the call ends; do not rely on "a local variable from the previous call".

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Python passes arguments "by value of the object reference":

 1def append_one(a: list[int]) -> None:
 2    a.append(1)       # modifies the shared object
 3
 4def rebind(a: list[int]) -> None:
 5    a = [99]          # rebinds only the local name; the caller is unaffected
 6
 7x = []
 8append_one(x)
 9print(x)              # [1]
10rebind(x)
11print(x)              # [1]

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
1#include <vector>
2
3void append_one(std::vector<int>& a) { a.push_back(1); } // reference: modifies the original object
4void rebind(std::vector<int> a) { a = {99}; }            // value: a copy
  • T: copied by value;
  • T&: a reference, which can modify the original object;
  • const T&: a read-only reference that avoids copying;
  • T*: a pointer, requiring null checks and attention to lifetime.

docs.title: Function Decomposition
docs.text:
Separate "read input, compute, write output", leaving the main function responsible only for the flow:

1def solve(a: list[int]) -> int:
2    return max(a) - min(a)
3
4def main() -> None:
5    n = int(input())
6    a = list(map(int, input().split()))
7    print(solve(a))

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note empty container the function must define its behaviour: throw, return None, or return a sentinel value modifying parameters document it clearly; C++ uses &, while in Python it depends on whether the object is mutable recursive function must have a base case; mind the recursion depth returning references in C++, never return a reference or pointer to a local variable

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Write min_max(a), which returns the minimum and the maximum together in a single pass.
  2. Write reverse_in_place(a) in both Python and C++, and state whether it modifies the original array.
  3. Write a recursive function and an iterative function to compute Fibonacci numbers, and compare their running time for \(n=35\).

docs.title: 1.5 Introduction to Arrays and Strings
docs.text: Level: Level 1 · Programming and Algorithms: Getting Started Status: expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Access, traverse and modify arrays through indices;
  • Distinguish Python list and str from C++ vector and string;
  • Know the copying cost caused by the immutability of strings.

docs.title: Arrays: Contiguous Storage and Indices
docs.text:
Python's list is an array of object references; C++'s vector<T> is a contiguously stored array of values.

1a = [10, 20, 30, 40]
2for i in range(len(a)):
3    a[i] += 1
4print(a)          # [11, 21, 31, 41]
5print(a[1:3])     # [21, 31], slicing produces a new list

1#include <iostream>
2#include <vector>
3
4int main() {
5    std::vector<int> a{10, 20, 30, 40};
6    for (int& x : a) ++x;              // reference: modifies the elements
7    for (int x : a) std::cout << x << ' ';
8    std::cout << '\n';
9}

docs.title: Traversal Styles
docs.text:
• Traversal by index: when the index is needed, when modification is needed, or when adjacent elements must be accessed;
  • Traversal by value: read-only, no modification;
  • Traversal by reference (C++): modifies the elements;
  • Python's enumerate yields both the index and the value.
1for i, x in enumerate(a):
2    print(i, x)

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
Python's str is immutable; every slice and every concatenation may create a new object.

1s = "algorithm"
2print(s[0], s[-1])      # a m
3print(s[1:4])           # lgo
4# s[0] = 'A'            # TypeError
5t = "A" + s[1:]         # creates a new string

C++'s std::string is mutable:

1#include <iostream>
2#include <string>
3
4int main() {
5    std::string s = "algorithm";
6    s[0] = 'A';
7    std::string t = s.substr(1, 3); // "lgo"
8    std::cout << s << ' ' << t << '\n';
9}

docs.title: Complexity of Concatenation
docs.text:
• Repeated s += ch inside a loop:
  • Python strings are immutable, so this may incur \(O(n^2)\) copying;
  • C++'s std::string has capacity and amortised growth, so it is usually close to \(O(n)\).
  • For heavy concatenation, prefer collecting the pieces in a list and then calling ''.join(parts).
1parts = []
2for ch in "algorithm":
3    parts.append(ch.upper())
4result = "".join(parts)

docs.title: Two-dimensional Arrays
docs.text:
In Python, only [[0] * m for _ in range(n)] yields independent rows; [[0] * m] * n shares the same row.

1n, m = 3, 4
2grid = [[0] * m for _ in range(n)]
3grid[0][0] = 1
4print(grid[1][0])  # 0, unaffected by the sharing

C++:

1#include <vector>
2
3int main() {
4    int n = 3, m = 4;
5    std::vector<std::vector<int>> grid(n, std::vector<int>(m, 0));
6}

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Empty array / empty string a[0] must not be accessed; check the length first Index out of range Python raises IndexError; in C++ an out-of-range access is undefined behaviour Negative index Supported in Python; not supported by C++ vector Slice boundaries a[l:r] includes l and excludes r String modification Python must create a new string; C++ can modify in place

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Reverse an array: use slicing, in-place two pointers and C++ std::reverse respectively.
  2. Count the occurrences of every character in a string; compare Python dict with C++ unordered_map.
  3. Given an \(n\times m\) matrix, output its transpose; compare \(O(nm)\) extra space with in-place rotation (square matrices).

docs.title: 1.6 References and Copying
docs.text: Level: Level 1 · Programming and Algorithms: Getting Started Status: expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Distinguish "name binding", "object sharing" and "copying an object";
  • Understand assignment, shallow copy and deep copy in Python;
  • Understand values, references, pointers and ownership in C++.

docs.title: Python: Assignment Does Not Copy Objects
docs.text:
1a = [1, 2, 3]
2b = a          # b and a are bound to the same list
3b.append(4)
4print(a)       # [1, 2, 3, 4]
5
6c = a.copy()   # shallow copy
7c.append(5)
8print(a)       # [1, 2, 3, 4]

With nested objects, a shallow copy copies only the outer level:

1import copy
2a = [[1], [2]]
3b = a.copy()
4b[0].append(9)
5print(a)          # [[1, 9], [2]]
6d = copy.deepcopy(a)
7d[1].append(8)
8print(a)          # [[1, 9], [2]]

docs.title: C++: Values, References and Pointers
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2#include <vector>
 3
 4int main() {
 5    std::vector<int> a{1, 2, 3};
 6    std::vector<int> b = a;        // value copy
 7    b.push_back(4);
 8    std::cout << a.size() << ' ' << b.size() << '\n'; // 3 4
 9
10    std::vector<int>& r = a;       // reference: the same object
11    r.push_back(5);
12    std::cout << a.size() << '\n'; // 4
13
14    std::vector<int>* p = &a;      // pointer: dereferencing and null checks are required
15    p->push_back(6);
16    std::cout << a.back() << '\n'; // 6
17}

docs.title: Ownership and Lifetime
docs.text:
• Stack objects are destroyed automatically when they leave their scope;
  • Objects created with new require delete (modern C++ prefers std::unique_ptr / std::shared_ptr);
  • A reference must be bound to a valid object and must not dangle;
  • Returning a reference or pointer to a local variable is an error.
1#include <memory>
2
3std::unique_ptr<int> make_value(int x) {
4    return std::make_unique<int>(x);
5}

docs.title: 1.7 Basic Simulation
docs.text: Level: Level 1 · Programming and Algorithms: Getting Started Status: expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Translate rules into states and state transitions;
  • Advance a simulation in time steps with loops;
  • Handle input, boundaries and termination conditions.

docs.title: The Three Parts of a Simulation
docs.text:
1. State: which variables describe the current situation completely;
  2. Rules: how each step derives the new state from the old one;
  3. Termination: how many steps to simulate, when to stop, and what to output.

docs.title: Example: A Robot Walking on a Grid
docs.text:
The robot starts at \((0,0)\) in an \(n\times m\) grid and moves according to the commands U/D/L/R; a command that would leave the grid is ignored. Output the final position and the number of distinct cells visited.

 1def simulate(n: int, m: int, commands: str) -> tuple[int, int, int]:
 2    r = c = 0
 3    visited = {(0, 0)}
 4    delta = {"U": (-1, 0), "D": (1, 0), "L": (0, -1), "R": (0, 1)}
 5    for ch in commands:
 6        if ch not in delta:
 7            continue
 8        dr, dc = delta[ch]
 9        nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
10        if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < m:
11            r, c = nr, nc
12            visited.add((r, c))
13    return r, c, len(visited)

C++ records the visited cells with a set<pair<int,int>>:

 1#include <set>
 2#include <string>
 3#include <utility>
 4
 5std::tuple<int,int,int> simulate(int n, int m, const std::string& commands) {
 6    int r = 0, c = 0;
 7    std::set<std::pair<int,int>> visited{{0, 0}};
 8    for (char ch : commands) {
 9        int dr = 0, dc = 0;
10        if (ch == 'U') dr = -1;
11        else if (ch == 'D') dr = 1;
12        else if (ch == 'L') dc = -1;
13        else if (ch == 'R') dc = 1;
14        else continue;
15        int nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc;
16        if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < m) {
17            r = nr; c = nc;
18            visited.insert({r, c});
19        }
20    }
21    return {r, c, static_cast<int>(visited.size())};
22}

docs.title: Example: One Step of the Game of Life
docs.text:
Rules: each cell looks at its 8 neighbours; a live cell dies if it has fewer than 2 or more than 3 live neighbours; a dead cell becomes alive if it has exactly 3 live neighbours.

 1def step(board: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
 2    n, m = len(board), len(board[0])
 3    nxt = [[0] * m for _ in range(n)]
 4    for i in range(n):
 5        for j in range(m):
 6            alive = 0
 7            for di in (-1, 0, 1):
 8                for dj in (-1, 0, 1):
 9                    if di == 0 and dj == 0:
10                        continue
11                    ni, nj = i + di, j + dj
12                    if 0 <= ni < n and 0 <= nj < m:
13                        alive += board[ni][nj]
14            if board[i][j] == 1:
15                nxt[i][j] = 1 if alive in (2, 3) else 0
16            else:
17                nxt[i][j] = 1 if alive == 3 else 0
18    return nxt

Time \(O(nm)\), extra space \(O(nm)\). Updating in place requires dealing with the mixing of the old and new states, which usually needs extra markers or double buffering.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Empty grid Return immediately when n=0 or m=0 Command leaving the grid Ignore it; the state does not change Invalid character Ignore it explicitly or report an error Number of simulation steps Fixed number of steps / until stable / detect a cycle State explosion Watch memory when recording visited states

docs.text:

  2. Implement a \(k\)-step simulation of "Conway's Game of Life" and output the number of live cells at each step.
  3. Design an "elevator scheduling" simulation and state its state, rules and termination conditions.

docs.title: 1.8 Debugging and Boundaries
docs.text: Level: Level 1 · Programming and Algorithms: Getting Started Status: expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Locate errors with assertions and minimal cases;
  • Systematically check empty input, duplicate values, out-of-range access, integer ranges and floating-point error;
  • Know that "it runs" does not mean "it is correct".

docs.title: Debugging Order
docs.text:
1. Reproduce: keep the minimal input;
  2. Shrink: delete irrelevant data;
  3. Observe: print the key state, not just the result;
  4. Hypothesise: propose one verifiable cause;
  5. Verify: change one thing and rerun;
  6. Regress: add the case to the tests so that it cannot reappear.
1def max_index(a: list[int]) -> int:
2    assert a, "max_index requires a non-empty list"
3    best = 0
4    for i in range(1, len(a)):
5        if a[i] > a[best]:
6            best = i
7    return best

docs.title: Empty Input
docs.text:
1def first(a):
2    if not a:
3        raise ValueError("empty")
4    return a[0]

docs.title: Duplicate Values
docs.text:
Should the first maximum or the last maximum be returned? This must be stated clearly and tested.

1def first_max(a: list[int]) -> int:
2    best = 0
3    for i in range(1, len(a)):
4        if a[i] > a[best]:  # strictly greater: keeps the first one
5            best = i
6    return best

docs.title: Out-of-range Access and Off-by-one
docs.text:
Binary search is the most prone to mixing up left <= right and left < right:

1def lower_bound(a: list[int], x: int) -> int:
2    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
3    while lo < hi:
4        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
5        if a[mid] < x:
6            lo = mid + 1
7        else:
8            hi = mid
9    return lo

Returns the position of the first element \(\ge x\); hi = len(a) allows returning n when all elements are less than \(x\).

docs.title: Integer Ranges
docs.text:
1def safe_sum(a: list[int]) -> int:
2    return sum(a)  # Python integers do not overflow

In C++ the upper bound must be estimated:

1#include <vector>
2
3long long sum(const std::vector<int>& a) {
4    long long s = 0;
5    for (int x : a) s += x;
6    return s;
7}

docs.title: Floating-point Error
docs.text:
1def close(a: float, b: float, eps: float = 1e-9) -> bool:
2    return abs(a - b) <= eps * max(1.0, abs(a), abs(b))

Do not compare computed results with ==; relative and absolute error must be considered together.

docs.title: Randomised Cross-checking
docs.text:
Use a brute-force solution to validate an optimised solution:

 1import random
 2
 3def brute(a):
 4    return max(a) if a else None
 5
 6def fast(a):
 7    return max(a) if a else None
 8
 9for _ in range(1000):
10    n = random.randint(0, 20)
11    a = [random.randint(-10, 10) for _ in range(n)]
12    assert brute(a) == fast(a), a

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] empty input, a single element, all elements equal;
  • [ ] minimum, maximum, negative numbers;
  • [ ] indices 0, n-1, n;
  • [ ] integer overflow and type conversion;
  • [ ] floating-point error and tolerance;
  • [ ] whether assertions are kept in release builds;
  • [ ] whether the error message is informative enough to locate the problem.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Write 10 boundary cases for summarize from Section 1.1.
  2. Implement upper_bound and explain how it differs from lower_bound.
  3. Use randomised cross-checking to verify that insertion sort produces the same results as sorted.

Goal: Understand correctness and efficiency, and be able to compare different solutions.

docs.title: Chapters

docs.title: Writing Conventions
docs.text:
• Present the problem and the interface first, then the implementation;
  • The Python version prioritizes expressing the algorithm structure;
  • The C++ version demonstrates pointers, memory layout, ownership, and resource management;
  • Each chapter includes at least: normal cases, boundary cases, complexity analysis, and exercises.

docs.title: 2.1 Problem Definition
docs.text: Level: Level 2 · Foundations of Algorithm Analysis Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Write a natural-language problem as inputs, outputs, constraints and valid results;
  • Describe a function contract with preconditions/postconditions;
  • Find ambiguities and boundary cases before implementation.

docs.title: A Complete Problem Definition
docs.text:
Take "range sum" as an example:

  • Input: an integer array \(a\) and indices \(l,r\) with \(0\le l\le r<n\);
  • Output: \(\sum_{i=l}^{r} a_i\);
  • Constraints: \(n\le 10^5\), \(|a_i|\le 10^9\);
  • Valid results: the range sum, which may exceed a 32-bit integer;
  • Invalid inputs: an empty array, \(l>r\), out of bounds.

Without these conventions, a program that merely "runs" still does not show that it is correct.

docs.title: Function Contract
docs.text:
1range_sum(a, l, r)
2pre:  0 <= l <= r < len(a)
3post: returns sum(a[l:r+1])

When a precondition is violated, the function may choose to:

  1. throw an exception;
  2. return an error code/None;
  3. fail an assertion (development only).

The choice must be consistent and documented clearly.

docs.title: Python Implementation
docs.text:
1def range_sum(a: list[int], l: int, r: int) -> int:
 2    """Return sum(a[l:r+1]); raise ValueError on invalid bounds."""
 3    if not (0 <= l <= r < len(a)):
 4        raise ValueError(f"invalid range [{l}, {r}] for length {len(a)}")
 5    total = 0
 6    for i in range(l, r + 1):
 7        total += a[i]
 8    return total
 9
10
11if __name__ == "__main__":
12    a = [3, -1, 4, 1, 5]
13    print(range_sum(a, 1, 3))  # 4

docs.title: C++ Implementation
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2#include <stdexcept>
 3#include <vector>
 4
 5long long range_sum(const std::vector<int>& a, int l, int r) {
 6    if (!(0 <= l && l <= r && r < static_cast<int>(a.size()))) {
 7        throw std::out_of_range("invalid range");
 8    }
 9    long long total = 0;
10    for (int i = l; i <= r; ++i) total += a[i];
11    return total;
12}
13
14int main() {
15    std::vector<int> a{3, -1, 4, 1, 5};
16    std::cout << range_sum(a, 1, 3) << '\n'; // 4
17}

docs.title: How Constraints Affect the Implementation
docs.text:
• If \(n\le 10^5\), a single \(O(n)\) sum is acceptable;
  • If \(10^5\) range queries are needed, a single \(O(n)\) sum becomes \(O(nq)\), so a prefix sum should be used;
  • If \(|a_i|\le10^9\) and \(n\le10^5\), a range sum can reach \(10^{14}\), so C++ must use long long.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Input Expected l=r sum of a single element a=[] invalid, throw an exception l<0 or r>=n invalid l>r invalid; must not silently return 0

  2. Change range_sum to return (sum, ok), and compare the exception style with the return-code style.
  3. Design a case where the input is valid but the result overflows, and explain why constraints must be written down.

docs.title: 2.2 Operation Count
docs.text: Level: Level 2 · Foundations of Algorithm Analysis Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Compare algorithms by their "number of basic operations";
  • Distinguish the input size \(n\), the iteration count and the actual running time;
  • Understand why halving the size produces \(\log n\).

docs.title: Basic Operations
docs.text:
First agree on what counts as one operation: comparison, assignment, arithmetic, array access. Different conventions change the constant factor but not the growth order.

1def linear_search(a: list[int], x: int) -> int:
2    ops = 0
3    for i, value in enumerate(a):
4        ops += 1          # comparison
5        if value == x:
6            return i, ops
7    return -1, ops

The worst case performs \(n\) comparisons; the best case 1; the average is about \(n/2\) (assuming equal probability and that the element exists).

docs.title: Halving the Size
docs.text:
1def binary_search(a: list[int], x: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
 2    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
 3    ops = 0
 4    while lo < hi:
 5        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
 6        ops += 1
 7        if a[mid] < x:
 8            lo = mid + 1
 9        else:
10            hi = mid
11    return lo, ops

Each round roughly halves the interval length: \(n,n/2,n/4,\dots,1\), for at most \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) rounds.

docs.title: Operation Counting in C++
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2#include <vector>
 3
 4std::pair<int,int> linear_search(const std::vector<int>& a, int x) {
 5    int ops = 0;
 6    for (int i = 0; i < static_cast<int>(a.size()); ++i) {
 7        ++ops;
 8        if (a[i] == x) return {i, ops};
 9    }
10    return {-1, ops};
11}
12
13int main() {
14    std::vector<int> a{1, 3, 5, 7, 9};
15    auto [i, ops] = linear_search(a, 7);
16    std::cout << i << ' ' << ops << '\n';
17}

docs.title: Common Iteration Counts
docs.text: Code shape Count Growth for i in range(n) \(n\) linear Nested for \(n^2\) quadratic while n > 1: n //= 2 \(\log_2 n\) logarithmic i *= 2 each round until \(n\) \(\log_2 n\) logarithmic Recursion \(T(n)=2T(n/2)+n\) \(n\log n\) linearithmic

docs.title: Boundaries and Caveats
docs.text:
• An operation count is a model, not real time; caches, branch prediction and interpreter overhead all affect the constant factor;
  • Best/worst/average cases must be stated separately;
  • For small \(n\), a lower-growth algorithm is not necessarily faster;
  • The counting code itself adds overhead; use it for analysis only and keep it out of production paths.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Add counting to binary search and verify that the operation count is about \(\log_2 n\) for \(n=10^3,10^6\).
  2. Write the operation-count formula for the triple loop \(\sum_{i<j<k}1\).
  3. Compare the iteration counts of "\(i+=1\) per round" and "\(i*=2\) per round".

docs.title: 2.3 Time Complexity
docs.text: Level: Level 2 · Foundations of Algorithm Analysis Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Use \(O,\Omega,\Theta\) to describe asymptotic upper bounds, lower bounds and tight bounds;
  • Identify constant, logarithmic, linear, linearithmic, quadratic and exponential growth;
  • Know that complexity notation drops constants but not the input size.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
For non-negative functions \(f,g\):

  • \(f(n)=O(g(n))\): there exist \(c>0,n_0\) such that \(f(n)\le cg(n)\) for \(n\ge n_0\);
  • \(f(n)=\Omega(g(n))\): there exist \(c>0,n_0\) such that \(f(n)\ge cg(n)\);
  • \(f(n)=\Theta(g(n))\): it is both \(O\) and \(\Omega\).

\(O\) is an upper bound, not an "exact time". Saying "this algorithm is \(O(n^2)\)" does not rule out that it is actually \(O(n)\).

docs.title: Common Growth Rates
docs.text: Complexity Typical source Intuition at \(n=10^6\) \(O(1)\) array indexing, hash average extremely fast \(O(\log n)\) binary search, balanced tree about 20 iterations \(O(n)\) a single pass \(10^6\) \(O(n\log n)\) merge/heap sort about \(2\times10^7\) \(O(n^2)\) nested loops \(10^{12}\), usually unacceptable \(O(2^n)\) subset enumeration only for very small inputs

docs.title: Code Comparison
docs.text:
1def constant(a: list[int]) -> int:
 2    return a[0] if a else -1
 3
 4def linear(a: list[int]) -> int:
 5    total = 0
 6    for x in a:
 7        total += x
 8    return total
 9
10def quadratic(a: list[int]) -> int:
11    count = 0
12    for i in range(len(a)):
13        for j in range(i + 1, len(a)):
14            count += 1
15    return count
16
17def logarithmic(n: int) -> int:
18    steps = 0
19    while n > 1:
20        n //= 2
21        steps += 1
22    return steps

C++:

 1#include <vector>
 2
 3long long linear(const std::vector<int>& a) {
 4    long long total = 0;
 5    for (int x : a) total += x;
 6    return total;
 7}
 8
 9long long quadratic(const std::vector<int>& a) {
10    long long count = 0;
11    for (int i = 0; i < static_cast<int>(a.size()); ++i)
12        for (int j = i + 1; j < static_cast<int>(a.size()); ++j)
13            ++count;
14    return count;
15}

docs.title: How to Count Nested Loops
docs.text:
1for i in 1..n:
2    for j in 1..i:
3        op

The count is \(\sum_{i=1}^n i=n(n+1)/2=\Theta(n^2)\).

1for i in 1..n:
2    for j in 1..n step i:
3        op

The count is \(n\sum_{i=1}^n 1/i=\Theta(n\log n)\) (harmonic series).

docs.title: Boundaries and Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Do not take the number of loop levels as the complexity; look at the count at each level;
  • The average case requires a probability assumption and cannot be assumed by default;
  • For recursion, count the call stack in the space usage;
  • An \(O(n)\) algorithm with a large constant may be slower than an \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm with a small constant;
  • Complexity is asymptotic; measure small scales in practice.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Determine the \(O,\Omega,\Theta\) of \(3n^2+5n+7\).
  2. Analyze the complexity of for i in range(n): for j in range(0,n,i+1).
  3. Prove that \(n!=\Omega(2^n)\) and explain what this means for enumeration algorithms.

docs.title: 2.4 Space Complexity
docs.text: Level: Level 2 · Foundations of Algorithm Analysis Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Distinguish input space, auxiliary space and output space;
  • Estimate the extra space of arrays, recursion stacks, hash tables and matrices;
  • Know that "in place" does not mean "zero space".

docs.title: Auxiliary Space
docs.text:
Space complexity usually refers to auxiliary space: the memory used in addition to the input and output.

  • Reversing an array in place: \(O(1)\) auxiliary space;
  • Copying an array: \(O(n)\);
  • Recursion depth \(n\): a call stack of \(O(n)\);
  • An \(n\times m\) matrix: \(O(nm)\).

docs.title: Code Comparison
docs.text:
1def reverse_in_place(a: list[int]) -> None:
2    i, j = 0, len(a) - 1
3    while i < j:
4        a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
5        i += 1
6        j -= 1
7
8def reverse_copy(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
9    return a[::-1]

C++:

 1#include <algorithm>
 2#include <vector>
 3
 4void reverse_in_place(std::vector<int>& a) {
 5    int i = 0, j = static_cast<int>(a.size()) - 1;
 6    while (i < j) std::swap(a[i++], a[j--]);
 7}
 8
 9std::vector<int> reverse_copy(const std::vector<int>& a) {
10    std::vector<int> b(a.rbegin(), a.rend());
11    return b;
12}

docs.title: The Recursion Stack
docs.text:
1def sum_recursive(a: list[int], i: int = 0) -> int:
2    if i == len(a):
3        return 0
4    return a[i] + sum_recursive(a, i + 1)

With recursion depth \(n\), each level stores its parameters and return address, so the auxiliary space is \(O(n)\). Rewriting it as a loop reduces this to \(O(1)\).

docs.title: Hash Tables and Strings
docs.text:
• Python dict/set use \(O(n)\) extra space on average, with load-factor and object overhead;
  • C++ unordered_map has bucket-array and node overhead;
  • String concatenation creates new objects; concatenating in a loop may accumulate \(O(n^2)\) temporary space.

docs.title: Trading Space for Time
docs.text: A prefix sum uses \(O(n)\) space to reduce a range query from \(O(n)\) to \(O(1)\). This is a typical trade-off; it is not that "less space is always better".

docs.title: Boundaries and Pitfalls
docs.text: Scenario Caveat Recursion depth \(10^5\) Python may raise RecursionError; C++ may overflow the stack 2D arrays n*m may be very large; use adjacency lists for sparse data Slicing/copying Python slicing creates a new list, not a view In-place algorithms May still use an \(O(\log n)\) stack or \(O(1)\) temporaries

docs.text:
1. Compare the space usage of the in-place and copying versions of array reversal.
  2. Write an \(O(1)\) auxiliary-space "remove duplicates from a sorted array".
  3. Analyze the auxiliary space of merge sort and explain why it is not strictly in-place.

docs.title: 2.5 Introduction to Correctness
docs.text: Level: Level 2 · Foundations of Algorithm Analysis Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Refute incorrect algorithms with counterexamples;
  • Prove iterative algorithms with loop invariants;
  • Prove recursive algorithms with induction;
  • Explain termination.

docs.title: Counterexamples
docs.text:
To prove an algorithm wrong, only one valid input that produces an incorrect output is needed.

1def wrong_max(a: list[int]) -> int:
2    best = 0
3    for x in a:
4        if x > best:
5            best = x
6    return best

Counterexample: [-3, -1, -2] returns 0, whereas the correct maximum is -1. Initializing best=0 implicitly assumes that "the array is nonnegative."

docs.title: Loop Invariants
docs.text:
Consider lower_bound binary search as an example:

1def lower_bound(a: list[int], x: int) -> int:
2    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
3    while lo < hi:
4        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
5        if a[mid] < x:
6            lo = mid + 1
7        else:
8            hi = mid
9    return lo

Invariants:

  1. The answer lies in \([lo,hi]\);
  2. a[0:lo] < x;
  3. a[hi:] >= x.

Each iteration:

  • If a[mid] < x, the answer cannot lie in [lo,mid]; set lo=mid+1;
  • Otherwise, the answer lies in [lo,mid]; set hi=mid.

At the end of the loop, lo==hi, and the invariants yield the answer.

docs.title: Termination
docs.text:
• hi-lo strictly decreases each iteration (mid < hi or lo=mid+1), so the loop terminates;
  • Recursion must have a base case, and each step must move toward that base case;
  • A while loop needs a measurable measure of progress.

docs.title: Induction
docs.text:
For the recursive sum:

1def sum_to(n: int) -> int:
2    if n == 0:
3        return 0
4    return n + sum_to(n - 1)

Proposition \(P(n)\): sum_to(n)=n(n+1)/2.

  • Base case: \(n=0\), which returns 0;
  • Induction step: Assume \(P(n-1)\); then sum_to(n)=n+(n-1)n/2=n(n+1)/2.

docs.title: C++ Version
docs.text:
1#include <vector>
 2
 3int lower_bound_cpp(const std::vector<int>& a, int x) {
 4    int lo = 0, hi = static_cast<int>(a.size());
 5    while (lo < hi) {
 6        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; // avoid overflow
 7        if (a[mid] < x) lo = mid + 1;
 8        else hi = mid;
 9    }
10    return lo;
11}

mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 is safer than (lo+hi)/2.

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text: Error Example Incorrect initialization Initialize the maximum to 0 Boundary error Mixing lo <= hi and lo < hi Non-termination The loop variable does not change Proving only some cases Forgetting empty arrays and duplicate values Incomplete loop invariant Not explaining the meaning of the interval

docs.text:
1. Write the complete invariant and termination proof for lower_bound.
  2. Find another counterexample to wrong_max, and fix it.
  3. Use induction to prove that the time complexity of sum_to is \(O(n)\).

docs.title: 2.6 Testing and Verification
docs.text: Level: Level 2 · Foundations of Algorithm Analysis Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Design normal cases, boundary cases, and randomized stress tests;
  • Use a naive solution as an oracle;
  • Understand that passing tests is not the same as proving correctness.

docs.title: Levels of Testing
docs.text:
1. Unit testing: a function's output on fixed inputs;
  2. Boundary testing: empty, single-element, duplicate, and extreme values;
  3. Randomized stress testing: small random inputs compared with a brute-force solution;
  4. Stress testing: large inputs, checking time/memory;
  5. Formal proof: loop invariants/induction.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Type Example Empty [], empty string Single element [0], [INT_MAX] Duplicates [1,1,1,1] Sorted/reverse-sorted Already sorted, completely reverse-sorted Extreme values Maximum/minimum integer, floating-point value close to 0 Invalid Out of bounds, l>r, non-numeric input

docs.title: Randomized Stress Testing
docs.text:
1import random
 2
 3def brute_max(a: list[int]) -> int | None:
 4    return max(a) if a else None
 5
 6def fast_max(a: list[int]) -> int | None:
 7    if not a:
 8        return None
 9    best = a[0]
10    for x in a[1:]:
11        if x > best:
12            best = x
13    return best
14
15for _ in range(5000):
16    n = random.randint(0, 30)
17    a = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(n)]
18    assert brute_max(a) == fast_max(a), a
19print("ok")

C++ randomized stress testing:

 1#include <algorithm>
 2#include <cassert>
 3#include <random>
 4#include <vector>
 5
 6int fast_max(const std::vector<int>& a) {
 7    int best = a[0];
 8    for (int x : a) best = std::max(best, x);
 9    return best;
10}
11
12int main() {
13    std::mt19937 rng(12345);
14    std::uniform_int_distribution<int> size(1, 30), value(-50, 50);
15    for (int t = 0; t < 5000; ++t) {
16        int n = size(rng);
17        std::vector<int> a(n);
18        for (int& x : a) x = value(rng);
19        assert(fast_max(a) == *std::max_element(a.begin(), a.end()));
20    }
21}

docs.title: Limitations of Testing
docs.text:
• Random testing covers only the sampling distribution;
  • The absence of a counterexample does not mean the algorithm is correct;
  • Assertions may be disabled in release builds;
  • Floating-point results require a tolerance.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Write 10 boundary cases for lower_bound.
  2. Use randomized stress testing to verify insertion sort against sorted.
  3. Design an off-by-one error that is "hard to find by random testing," and explain how to construct a targeted case.

docs.title: 2.7 Performance Measurement
docs.text: Level: Level 2 · Foundations of Algorithm Analysis Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Use timeit / chrono for basic measurements;
  • Distinguish theoretical complexity, constants, input distributions, and cache effects;
  • Understand that microbenchmarks can easily mislead.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Before Measuring
docs.text:
1. Which operation is being measured?
  2. What are the input size and distribution?
  3. Does the measurement include I/O, initialization, or compilation/interpretation overhead?
  4. Is it repeated enough times?
  5. Can the results be explained by complexity?

docs.title: Python: timeit
docs.text:
1import timeit
2
3setup = "a = list(range(1000))"
4print(timeit.timeit("sum(a)", setup=setup, number=10000))
5print(timeit.timeit("total = 0\nfor x in a:\n    total += x", setup=setup, number=10000))

sum is a C-level loop and is usually significantly faster than a Python-level loop; this reflects a constant-factor difference, and both are still \(O(n)\).

docs.title: C++: chrono
docs.text:
1#include <chrono>
 2#include <iostream>
 3#include <numeric>
 4#include <vector>
 5
 6int main() {
 7    std::vector<int> a(1000000, 1);
 8    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
 9    long long s = 0;
10    for (int x : a) s += x;
11    auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
12    auto us = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds>(t1 - t0).count();
13    std::cout << s << " " << us << "us\n";
14}

docs.title: Input Distribution
docs.text:
The same algorithm can differ greatly across inputs:

  • Insertion sort: \(O(n)\) on sorted input, \(O(n^2)\) on reverse-sorted input;
  • Quicksort: expected \(O(n\log n)\) with random pivoting, \(O(n^2)\) with extreme pivoting;
  • Hash table: \(O(1)\) on average, \(O(n)\) in the worst case.

When reporting performance, the input distribution must be stated.

docs.title: Microbenchmark Pitfalls
docs.text:
• The compiler may optimize away the result;
  • Cache warm-up, JIT, and Python interpreter state affect the results;
  • Measurement granularity is too coarse (measuring microsecond operations at millisecond granularity);
  • Measuring only once, so noise is high;
  • Different machines/compilers cannot be compared directly.

docs.title: Simple Experiment
docs.text:
1import timeit
2for n in (100, 1000, 10000):
3    a = list(range(n))
4    t = timeit.timeit(lambda: sum(a), number=1000)
5    print(n, t)

Observe the growth trend, not just a single point.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Compare the elapsed time of sum and a hand-written loop at \(n=10^3,10^5,10^6\).
  2. Measure the differences in insertion sort on sorted/reverse-sorted/random inputs.
  3. Design a microbenchmark that shows how "the compiler optimizing away the result" can mislead conclusions.

docs.title: 3.1 Storage and Nodes
docs.text: Level: Level 3 · Basic Data Structures Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Distinguish contiguous storage from linked storage;
  • Connect nodes with object references/pointers;
  • Understand lifetime, ownership, and resource management in C++.

docs.title: Contiguous Storage vs Linked Storage
docs.text:
Contiguous storage: elements are adjacent in memory, index access is \(O(1)\), and insertion or deletion may move a large number of elements. Linked storage: each node stores data and a reference to the next node; insertion and deletion only require changing links, but accessing the \(k\)-th element requires walking \(k\) steps.

Operation Contiguous array Linked list Access by index \(O(1)\) \(O(n)\) Insert at head \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Insert after a known node \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Space overhead Compact One extra pointer per node

docs.title: Python: Object References
docs.text:
1class Node:
2    def __init__(self, value: int, next: "Node | None" = None) -> None:
3        self.value = value
4        self.next = next
5
6a = Node(1)
7b = Node(2)
8a.next = b          # a references b
9print(a.next.value) # 2

Python variables hold object references; a.next = b does not copy b, it only adds a reference.

docs.title: C++: Values, Pointers, and Ownership
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2#include <memory>
 3
 4struct Node {
 5    int value;
 6    std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
 7    explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
 8};
 9
10int main() {
11    auto a = std::make_unique<Node>(1);
12    a->next = std::make_unique<Node>(2);
13    std::cout << a->next->value << '\n'; // 2
14}

std::unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership: when a is destroyed, the entire chain is released recursively. Do not use a raw new and then forget delete.

docs.title: Raw Pointer Version
docs.text:
1struct Node {
2    int value;
3    Node* next;
4};

A raw pointer does not express ownership, so "who is responsible for freeing" must be made explicit; dangling pointers, double frees, and memory leaks are easy to introduce.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Empty chain The head pointer is nullptr / None Deleting a node Save next first, then free the current node Shared nodes C++ requires shared_ptr or an explicit statement of non-ownership Cycles Traversal may loop forever; a visited set or fast/slow pointers are needed

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Build a three-node chain in both Python and C++, and print it in forward order.
  2. Explain why "inserting at the head of a linked list is \(O(1)\)" but "deleting the node whose value is x" is usually \(O(n)\).
  3. Implement a chain with unique_ptr and verify that no memory is leaked on destruction (a sanitizer may be used).

docs.title: 3.2 Dynamic Array
docs.text: Level: Level 3 · Basic Data Structures Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Implement a dynamic array with capacity and length;
  • Understand resizing and amortized cost;
  • Know why insertion/deletion is \(O(n)\).

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
1size()       current number of elements
2get(i)       access by index
3push_back(x) insert at the end
4pop_back()   remove the last element
5insert(i,x)  insert at position i
6erase(i)     remove at position i

docs.title: Python Teaching Implementation
docs.text:
1class DynamicArray:
 2    def __init__(self, capacity: int = 1) -> None:
 3        self._data = [None] * capacity
 4        self._size = 0
 5        self._capacity = capacity
 6
 7    def __len__(self) -> int:
 8        return self._size
 9
10    def get(self, i: int) -> int:
11        if not 0 <= i < self._size:
12            raise IndexError(i)
13        return self._data[i]
14
15    def push_back(self, x: int) -> None:
16        if self._size == self._capacity:
17            self._resize(self._capacity * 2)
18        self._data[self._size] = x
19        self._size += 1
20
21    def _resize(self, new_cap: int) -> None:
22        new_data = [None] * new_cap
23        for i in range(self._size):
24            new_data[i] = self._data[i]
25        self._data = new_data
26        self._capacity = new_cap

docs.title: C++ Teaching Implementation
docs.text:
1#include <algorithm>
 2#include <stdexcept>
 3#include <vector>
 4
 5class DynamicArray {
 6    int* data_ = nullptr;
 7    int size_ = 0;
 8    int capacity_ = 0;
 9
10public:
11    explicit DynamicArray(int cap = 1) : data_(new int[cap]), capacity_(cap) {}
12    ~DynamicArray() { delete[] data_; }
13    DynamicArray(const DynamicArray&) = delete;
14    DynamicArray& operator=(const DynamicArray&) = delete;
15
16    int size() const { return size_; }
17    int get(int i) const {
18        if (i < 0 || i >= size_) throw std::out_of_range("index");
19        return data_[i];
20    }
21    void push_back(int x) {
22        if (size_ == capacity_) resize(capacity_ * 2);
23        data_[size_++] = x;
24    }
25    void resize(int cap) {
26        int* next = new int[cap];
27        std::copy(data_, data_ + size_, next);
28        delete[] data_;
29        data_ = next;
30        capacity_ = cap;
31    }
32};

Real projects use std::vector directly; this version demonstrates capacity, copying, and release.

docs.title: Amortized Analysis
docs.text:
Starting from capacity 1 and calling push_back repeatedly: resizing happens at 1, 2, 4, 8, …, and the total number of copies is

\[ 1+2+4+\cdots+n<2n. \]

The total cost of \(n\) insertions is \(O(n)\), so the amortized cost per insertion is \(O(1)\).

docs.title: Insertion and Deletion
docs.text: Inserting at index \(i\) requires shifting \([i,n)\) one position to the right, which is \(O(n)\) in the worst case; deletion is analogous. Only insertion/deletion at the end is \(O(1)\) amortized.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Empty array pop_back must check Zero capacity Use an initial capacity of at least 1, or handle it separately Resizing failure C++ new may throw bad_alloc Iterator invalidation After a vector resize, old iterators/pointers are invalidated

docs.text:
1. Add insert and erase, and analyze their worst-case complexity.
  2. Implement "shrinking": halve the capacity when the number of elements is below 1/4 of capacity, and explain why the threshold is not 1/2.
  3. Compare the resizing strategies of DynamicArray and std::vector.

docs.title: 3.3 Linked List
docs.text: Level: Level 3 · Basic Data Structures Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Implement singly and doubly linked lists;
  • Insert/delete at a known position;
  • Reverse a linked list and analyze the pointer operations.

docs.title: Singly Linked List Node
docs.text:
1class Node:
2    def __init__(self, value: int, next: "Node | None" = None) -> None:
3        self.value = value
4        self.next = next

C++:

1struct Node {
2    int value;
3    Node* next;
4    explicit Node(int v) : value(v), next(nullptr) {}
5};

docs.title: Push Front and Traversal
docs.text:
1def push_front(head: Node | None, x: int) -> Node:
2    return Node(x, head)
3
4def to_list(head: Node | None) -> list[int]:
5    out = []
6    while head:
7        out.append(head.value)
8        head = head.next
9    return out

Push front is \(O(1)\); traversal is \(O(n)\); deletion by value is usually \(O(n)\).

docs.title: Deleting Nodes
docs.text:
1def remove_value(head: Node | None, x: int) -> Node | None:
2    dummy = Node(0, head)
3    cur = dummy
4    while cur.next:
5        if cur.next.value == x:
6            cur.next = cur.next.next
7        else:
8            cur = cur.next
9    return dummy.next

The sentinel node dummy unifies "deleting the head node" and "deleting an interior node".

docs.title: Reversing a Linked List
docs.text:
1def reverse(head: Node | None) -> Node | None:
2    prev = None
3    cur = head
4    while cur:
5        nxt = cur.next
6        cur.next = prev
7        prev = cur
8        cur = nxt
9    return prev

Three steps: save next, redirect the link, advance prev/cur. Time \(O(n)\), space \(O(1)\).

docs.title: Complete C++ Example
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2
 3struct Node {
 4    int value;
 5    Node* next;
 6    explicit Node(int v) : value(v), next(nullptr) {}
 7};
 8
 9Node* reverse(Node* head) {
10    Node* prev = nullptr;
11    while (head) {
12        Node* next = head->next;
13        head->next = prev;
14        prev = head;
15        head = next;
16    }
17    return prev;
18}
19
20int main() {
21    Node* head = new Node(1);
22    head->next = new Node(2);
23    head->next->next = new Node(3);
24    head = reverse(head);
25    for (Node* p = head; p; p = p->next) std::cout << p->value << ' ';
26    while (head) { Node* n = head->next; delete head; head = n; }
27}

docs.title: Doubly Linked List
docs.text: A doubly linked list node stores both prev and next; given a node, deletion is \(O(1)\), at the cost of extra pointers and maintenance overhead. Head and tail sentinels can further unify the boundary cases.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Empty chain Return nullptr/None Deleting the head Use a dummy or handle it separately Deleting the tail A singly linked list must find the predecessor, \(O(n)\) Cycles Traversal loops forever; detect with fast/slow pointers

  2. Use fast/slow pointers to find the middle of a linked list.
  3. Determine whether a linked list has a cycle, and return the entry point of the cycle.

docs.title: 3.4 Stack
docs.text: Level: Level 3 · Basic Data Structures Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand last in, first out (LIFO);
  • Use a stack for bracket matching and expression handling;
  • Know the \(O(1)\) operations and space cost of a stack.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
1push(x)  push onto the stack
2pop()    pop the top of the stack
3top()    inspect the top of the stack
4empty()  whether the stack is empty

docs.title: Python Implementation
docs.text:
1class Stack:
 2    def __init__(self) -> None:
 3        self._data: list[int] = []
 4
 5    def push(self, x: int) -> None:
 6        self._data.append(x)
 7
 8    def pop(self) -> int:
 9        if not self._data:
10            raise IndexError("pop from empty stack")
11        return self._data.pop()
12
13    def top(self) -> int:
14        if not self._data:
15            raise IndexError("top from empty stack")
16        return self._data[-1]
17
18    def empty(self) -> bool:
19        return not self._data

docs.title: C++ Implementation
docs.text:
1#include <stdexcept>
 2#include <vector>
 3
 4class Stack {
 5    std::vector<int> data_;
 6public:
 7    void push(int x) { data_.push_back(x); }
 8    int pop() {
 9        if (data_.empty()) throw std::underflow_error("empty");
10        int x = data_.back();
11        data_.pop_back();
12        return x;
13    }
14    int top() const {
15        if (data_.empty()) throw std::underflow_error("empty");
16        return data_.back();
17    }
18    bool empty() const { return data_.empty(); }
19};

docs.title: Bracket Matching
docs.text:
1def is_balanced(s: str) -> bool:
 2    pairs = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}
 3    stack = []
 4    for ch in s:
 5        if ch in "([{":
 6            stack.append(ch)
 7        elif ch in pairs:
 8            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
 9                return False
10    return not stack

Time \(O(n)\), worst-case space \(O(n)\) (all opening brackets).

docs.title: Expression Evaluation
docs.text: For postfix (reverse Polish) expressions, push a number when one is encountered, and when an operator is encountered pop two numbers, compute, and push the result back. The stack makes the "most recent operands" naturally available.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note pop/top on an empty stack Throw an exception or return an error code; must not go out of bounds Only closing brackets Fail immediately Only opening brackets The stack is non-empty at the end, so fail Recursion depth The system call stack can also overflow

docs.text:
1. Use a stack to determine whether a string is a palindrome (ignoring non-letters).
  2. Implement postfix expression evaluation, handling division by zero.
  3. Implement a queue using two stacks.

docs.title: 3.5 Recursion and the Call Stack
docs.text: Level: Level 3 · Basic Data Structures Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Write the base case and the recursive step clearly;
  • Explain the space cost with the call stack;
  • Convert recursion into iteration.

docs.title: The Three Elements of Recursion
docs.text:
1. Base case: no further recursion;
  2. Recursive step: move toward the base case;
  3. Combination: combine the results of the subproblems into the result of the original problem.
1def factorial(n: int) -> int:
2    if n < 0:
3        raise ValueError("n must be non-negative")
4    if n == 0:
5        return 1
6    return n * factorial(n - 1)

Time \(O(n)\), call-stack space \(O(n)\).

docs.title: The Call Stack
docs.text:
Calling factorial(4):

1factorial(4)
2  factorial(3)
3    factorial(2)
4      factorial(1)
5        factorial(0) -> 1

Each level stores the arguments, the return address and the local variables. A recursion that is too deep overflows the stack; Python's default recursion depth is about 1000.

docs.title: Recursion vs Iteration
docs.text:
1def factorial_iter(n: int) -> int:
2    result = 1
3    for i in range(2, n + 1):
4        result *= i
5    return result

The iterative version uses \(O(1)\) auxiliary space and is usually faster; the recursive version stays closer to the mathematical definition.

docs.title: Tail Recursion Is Not a Cure-All
docs.text: Some languages support tail-call optimization; Python does not. A C++ compiler may optimize it, but you cannot rely on that. For deep recursion, prefer converting to iteration or an explicit stack.

docs.title: C++ Example
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2#include <stdexcept>
 3
 4long long factorial(int n) {
 5    if (n < 0) throw std::invalid_argument("negative");
 6    if (n == 0) return 1;
 7    return n * factorial(n - 1);
 8}
 9
10int main() {
11    std::cout << factorial(10) << '\n';
12}

docs.title: Recursion Tree
docs.text:
The naive recursive Fibonacci:

1def fib(n: int) -> int:
2    if n < 2:
3        return n
4    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

The number of calls is about \(O(2^n)\); memoization or iteration reduces it to \(O(n)\).

docs.title: Explicit Stack
docs.text: Rewriting recursion with an explicit stack lets you control the depth and avoids overflowing the system stack; the price is more complicated code.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note n=0 The base case must cover it Negative numbers Decide explicitly whether to throw or to return Depth \(10^5\) Iteration / explicit stack Overlapping subproblems Memoization

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Compute the factorial both recursively and iteratively, and compare their behavior at \(n=1000\).
  2. Use memoization to reduce fib to \(O(n)\).

docs.title: 3.6 Queue and Deque
docs.text: Level: Level 3 · Basic Data Structures Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand first in, first out (FIFO);
  • Implement a queue with a circular array;
  • Distinguish queue, deque and priority queue.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
1push_back(x)   enqueue
2pop_front()    dequeue
3front()        front of the queue
4back()         back of the queue
5empty()

docs.title: Circular Queue
docs.text:
Use an array of length cap, with head pointing at the front and size recording the number of elements:

 1class CircularQueue:
 2    def __init__(self, capacity: int) -> None:
 3        if capacity <= 0:
 4            raise ValueError("capacity must be positive")
 5        self._data = [0] * capacity
 6        self._head = 0
 7        self._size = 0
 8
 9    def push(self, x: int) -> None:
10        if self._size == len(self._data):
11            raise OverflowError("queue full")
12        tail = (self._head + self._size) % len(self._data)
13        self._data[tail] = x
14        self._size += 1
15
16    def pop(self) -> int:
17        if self._size == 0:
18            raise IndexError("queue empty")
19        x = self._data[self._head]
20        self._head = (self._head + 1) % len(self._data)
21        self._size -= 1
22        return x

Time \(O(1)\), space \(O(\text{capacity})\).

docs.title: C++ Circular Queue
docs.text:
1#include <stdexcept>
 2#include <vector>
 3
 4class CircularQueue {
 5    std::vector<int> data_;
 6    int head_ = 0;
 7    int size_ = 0;
 8public:
 9    explicit CircularQueue(int cap) : data_(cap) {}
10    void push(int x) {
11        if (size_ == static_cast<int>(data_.size())) throw std::overflow_error("full");
12        int tail = (head_ + size_) % data_.size();
13        data_[tail] = x;
14        ++size_;
15    }
16    int pop() {
17        if (size_ == 0) throw std::underflow_error("empty");
18        int x = data_[head_];
19        head_ = (head_ + 1) % data_.size();
20        --size_;
21        return x;
22    }
23};

docs.title: Standard Library
docs.text:
• Python: collections.deque, with \(O(1)\) operations at both ends;
  • C++: std::deque supports insertion and deletion at both ends, and std::queue is a container adapter;
  • A priority queue is not FIFO; see the heap chapter.

docs.title: Deque
docs.text: A deque supports push_front, push_back, pop_front and pop_back, and is often used for sliding windows and for 0-1 shortest paths in BFS.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Queue full Throw an exception, block, or overwrite — the interface must be explicit Queue empty pop is not allowed Capacity 0 Illegal Circular indices Use % capacity; do not go out of bounds

docs.text:

  2. Implement a fixed-capacity circular queue and write full/empty tests.
  3. Implement the sliding-window maximum with a deque.

docs.title: 3.7 Hash Table and Set
docs.text: Level: Level 3 · Basic Data Structures Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Map keys to buckets with a hash function;
  • Handle collisions and the load factor;
  • Distinguish the average \(O(1)\) from the worst-case \(O(n)\).

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A hash table consists of a bucket array and a hash function:

1index = hash(key) mod m

Different keys may land in the same bucket; this is called a collision. Common approaches:

  • Separate chaining: each bucket holds a linked list;
  • Open addressing: linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing.

docs.title: Python Separate Chaining
docs.text:
1class HashTable:
 2    def __init__(self, buckets: int = 8) -> None:
 3        self._buckets: list[list[tuple[int, int]]] = [[] for _ in range(buckets)]
 4        self._size = 0
 5
 6    def _index(self, key: int) -> int:
 7        return hash(key) % len(self._buckets)
 8
 9    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
10        bucket = self._buckets[self._index(key)]
11        for i, (k, _) in enumerate(bucket):
12            if k == key:
13                bucket[i] = (key, value)
14                return
15        bucket.append((key, value))
16        self._size += 1
17
18    def get(self, key: int) -> int | None:
19        for k, v in self._buckets[self._index(key)]:
20            if k == key:
21                return v
22        return None

Average \(O(1)\); in the worst case, when all keys collide, \(O(n)\).

docs.title: C++ Standard Library
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
2#include <string>
3#include <unordered_map>
4
5int main() {
6    std::unordered_map<std::string, int> freq;
7    for (std::string w : {"a", "b", "a"}) ++freq[w];
8    std::cout << freq["a"] << '\n'; // 2
9}

unordered_map does not preserve order; when order is needed, use std::map (\(O(\log n)\)).

docs.title: Load Factor and Resizing
docs.text: The load factor is \(\alpha=n/m\). With separate chaining, the table is usually resized once \(\alpha\) exceeds about 1; with open addressing, \(\alpha<0.7\) is usually maintained. Resizing requires rehashing all keys, which costs \(O(n)\) once, while the amortized cost remains \(O(1)\).

docs.title: Requirements for Hash Functions
docs.text:
• The same key must hash to the same value every time;
  • The distribution should be as uniform as possible;
  • It must be consistent with equality: if a == b, then hash(a) == hash(b);
  • Do not let mutable fields participate in hashing.

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Key does not exist Return None/end(); do not insert by default Many collisions Worst case \(O(n)\); exploitable by malicious input Resizing Iterators/references may be invalidated Floating-point/custom types A hash and an equality must be defined

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Add resizing and rehashing to HashTable.
  2. Find the first element in an array that occurs only once.
  3. Compare the average/worst-case complexity of dict, set, unordered_map and map.
