docs.title: 9.6 Algorithm Lower Bounds
docs.text: Level: Level 9 · Algorithm Theory and Computational Limits Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Prove the comparison-sorting lower bound with decision trees;
  • Understand the adversary argument;
  • Distinguish "lower bound" from "optimal algorithm".

docs.title: Comparison-Sorting Lower Bound
docs.text:
The decision tree of comparison sorting has \(n!\) leaves; the height of a binary tree is at least \(\log_2(n!)=\Omega(n\log n)\).

Therefore any comparison-based sort requires at least \(\Omega(n\log n)\) comparisons in the worst case.

docs.title: Counting Comparisons
docs.text:
1def insertion_sort_count(a: list[int]) -> tuple[list[int], int]:
 2    a = a[:]
 3    cmp = 0
 4    for i in range(1, len(a)):
 5        x = a[i]
 6        j = i - 1
 7        while j >= 0:
 8            cmp += 1
 9            if a[j] <= x:
10                break
11            a[j+1] = a[j]
12            j -= 1
13        a[j+1] = x
14    return a, cmp

For a reverse-ordered array the number of comparisons is \(\Theta(n^2)\); a lower bound only states "at least", not that some algorithm attains it.

docs.title: Adversary Argument
docs.text: The adversary answers each query so that the algorithm keeps as many possibilities as possible; if only a constant fraction can be eliminated each time, at least \(\Omega(\log N)\) queries are needed.

docs.title: Other Lower Bounds
docs.text:
• Searching an unordered array: \(\Omega(n)\);
  • Finding the maximum in the comparison model: \(n-1\) comparisons;
  • Some data-structure operations have amortised lower bounds.

docs.title: C++ Comparison Counting
docs.text:
1#include <algorithm>
 2#include <iostream>
 3#include <vector>
 4
 5int main() {
 6    std::vector<int> a{5,4,3,2,1};
 7    int cmp = 0;
 8    std::sort(a.begin(), a.end(), [&](int x, int y) { ++cmp; return x < y; });
 9    std::cout << cmp << '\n';
10}

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Non-comparison sorting the lower bound does not apply Worst case/average case lower bounds usually refer to the worst case Model RAM/comparison/Turing machine differ Lower-bound proof is not the same as an algorithm implementation

docs.text:
1. Prove the lower bound for searching an unordered array with a decision tree.
  2. Explain why counting sort does not violate \(\Omega(n\log n)\).
  3. Design an adversary strategy to prove a lower bound for some problem.

docs.title: 9.7 Approximation Algorithms
docs.text: Level: Level 9 · Algorithm Theory and Computational Limits Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Define the approximation ratio;
  • Write a 2-approximation for vertex cover;
  • Use a greedy approach for set cover.

docs.title: Approximation Ratio
docs.text:
For a minimisation problem, the algorithm's solution \(A\) and the optimal solution \(OPT\) satisfy

\[ A\le \rho\cdot OPT \]

and the algorithm is called a \(\rho\)-approximation. The closer \(\rho\) is to 1, the better.

docs.title: 2-Approximation for Vertex Cover
docs.text:
Repeatedly take an uncovered edge and add both of its endpoints to the cover.

 1def vertex_cover_2approx(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int,int]]) -> set[int]:
 2    cover = set()
 3    used = [False] * len(edges)
 4    for i, (u, v) in enumerate(edges):
 5        if used[i]:
 6            continue
 7        cover.add(u); cover.add(v)
 8        for j, (a, b) in enumerate(edges):
 9            if a in cover or b in cover:
10                used[j] = True
11    return cover

Approximation ratio 2: the edge chosen at each step has at least one endpoint that must lie in any cover, while we choose two.

docs.title: Greedy Set Cover
docs.text: At each step choose the set covering the most uncovered elements; the approximation ratio is \(H_n=O(\log n)\).

docs.title: C++ Vertex Cover
docs.text:
1#include <set>
 2#include <utility>
 3#include <vector>
 4
 5std::set<int> vertex_cover(const std::vector<std::pair<int,int>>& edges) {
 6    std::set<int> cover;
 7    for (auto [u, v] : edges) {
 8        if (cover.count(u) || cover.count(v)) continue;
 9        cover.insert(u); cover.insert(v);
10    }
11    return cover;
12}

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Maximisation problems the ratio points the other way Approximation ratio a worst-case guarantee Heuristics no guarantee, so not an approximation algorithm Inapproximability some problems have lower bounds

docs.title: 9.8 Online Algorithms
docs.text: Level: Level 9 · Algorithm Theory and Computational Limits Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand online decisions and the competitive ratio;
  • Analyse ski rental;
  • Understand cache replacement.

docs.title: Competitive Ratio
docs.text:
An online algorithm \(ALG\) and the offline optimum \(OPT\) satisfy

\[ ALG\le c\cdot OPT \]

which is called \(c\)-competitive. The input order is unknown and there is no going back.

docs.title: Ski Rental
docs.text:
A skier pays 1 each time to rent skis and \(B\) to buy them. They do not know how many times they will ski.

Strategy: rent first \(B-1\) times, then buy.

  • If the total number of times is \(<B\): the cost is \(k\le B-1\), and the optimum is also \(k\);
  • If the total number of times is \(\ge B\): the cost is \((B-1)+B=2B-1\), and the optimum is \(B\);
  • The competitive ratio is \(<2\).
1def ski_rental(days: int, buy: int) -> int:
2    cost = 0
3    for _ in range(days):
4        if cost < buy - 1:
5            cost += 1
6        else:
7            return cost + buy
8    return cost

docs.title: Cache Replacement
docs.text:
• FIFO/LRU: deterministic;
  • Random marking algorithm: \(O(\log k)\)-competitive;
  • The offline optimum needs knowledge of the future.

docs.title: Simplified LRU in C++
docs.text:
1#include <list>
 2#include <unordered_map>
 3
 4class LRU {
 5    int cap;
 6    std::list<int> order;
 7    std::unordered_map<int, std::list<int>::iterator> pos;
 8public:
 9    explicit LRU(int c) : cap(c) {}
10    void access(int x) {
11        if (pos.count(x)) order.erase(pos[x]);
12        else if (static_cast<int>(order.size()) == cap) { pos.erase(order.back()); order.pop_back(); }
13        order.push_front(x);
14        pos[x] = order.begin();
15    }
16};

docs.title: Boundary Cases
docs.text: Scenario Note Input order An online algorithm cannot reorder the input Competitive ratio Worst case Randomization Expected competitive ratio Cache size Special-case \(k=0\)

docs.text:
1. Prove the competitive ratio of ski rental.
  2. Compare the worst cases of FIFO and LRU.
  3. Design an online scheduling strategy and analyse its competitive ratio.

docs.title: 9.9 Parameterized Algorithms
docs.text: Level: Level 9 · Algorithm Theory and Computational Limits Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Define FPT;
  • Solve vertex cover with a search tree;
  • Understand kernelization.

docs.title: Parameterized Complexity
docs.text:
A problem instance carries a parameter \(k\); if the running time of the algorithm is

\[ O(f(k)\cdot n^c) \]

where \(c\) is independent of \(k\), the problem is called fixed-parameter tractable (FPT).

docs.title: Vertex Cover Search Tree
docs.text:
Pick an edge \((u,v)\); every cover must contain \(u\) or \(v\):

 1def vertex_cover_fpt(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int,int]], k: int) -> set[int] | None:
 2    if not edges:
 3        return set()
 4    if k == 0:
 5        return None
 6    u, v = edges[0]
 7    rest = [e for e in edges if u not in e and v not in e]
 8    left = vertex_cover_fpt(n, rest, k - 1)
 9    if left is not None:
10        return left | {u}
11    right = vertex_cover_fpt(n, rest, k - 1)
12    if right is not None:
13        return right | {v}
14    return None

Time \(O(2^k\cdot m)\).

docs.title: Kernelization
docs.text: Use rules to shrink the instance to a kernel whose size depends only on \(k\); for example, in vertex cover any vertex of degree \(>k\) must be selected.

docs.title: C++ Recursion Framework
docs.text:
1#include <utility>
 2#include <vector>
 3
 4bool vc(int k, std::vector<std::pair<int,int>> edges) {
 5    if (edges.empty()) return true;
 6    if (k == 0) return false;
 7    auto [u, v] = edges.front();
 8    std::vector<std::pair<int,int>> rest;
 9    for (auto e : edges) if (e.first != u && e.second != u && e.first != v && e.second != v) rest.push_back(e);
10    return vc(k-1, rest);
11}

(The example explores only one side; the complete version must try \(u\) and \(v\) separately.)

docs.text: Level: Level 9 · Algorithm Theory and Computational Limits Status: Expanded.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Distinguish Monte Carlo / Las Vegas;
  • Define RP, BPP, ZPP;
  • Lower the error rate by repeating the majority vote.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
• RP: polynomial time; when the correct answer is "yes" it accepts with probability at least \(1/2\); on "no" it always rejects;
  • coRP: one-sided guarantee for "no";
  • ZPP: Las Vegas, expected polynomial time, always-correct result;
  • BPP: two-sided error, error rate \(\le1/3\).
\[ RP\subseteq BPP,\qquad ZPP=RP\cap coRP. \]

docs.title: Error Amplification
docs.text:
If the single-run error rate is \(p<1/2\), independently repeating \(2t+1\) times and taking the majority makes the error rate decrease exponentially (Chernoff).

1import random
2
3def majority_vote(f, trials: int = 101) -> bool:
4    return sum(f() for _ in range(trials)) * 2 > trials

docs.title: Example: Randomized Primality Testing
docs.text: Miller–Rabin is Monte Carlo: a composite number may be misjudged as prime, and repeating \(k\) times lowers the error rate to \(4^{-k}\).

docs.title: C++ Repeated Experiment
docs.text:
1#include <iostream>
 2#include <random>
 3
 4int main() {
 5    std::mt19937 rng(12345);
 6    std::bernoulli_distribution coin(0.5);
 7    int yes = 0, trials = 10000;
 8    for (int i = 0; i < trials; ++i) yes += coin(rng);
 9    std::cout << static_cast<double>(yes) / trials << '\n';
10}
